concepts.name: Capturing tasks in a list
concepts.summary: Recall that writing every task in one trusted place frees working memory and prevents forgotten commitments.

concepts.name: Deadlines versus importance
concepts.summary: Explain the difference between a task being urgent (time-pressured) and important (valuable to your goals).

concepts.name: Estimating task duration
concepts.summary: Understand that tasks take time and that giving each a rough duration makes planning realistic.

concepts.name: Calendar as commitment record
concepts.summary: Recall that a calendar holds fixed-time commitments such as appointments and deadlines.

concepts.name: Common distractions
concepts.summary: Identify typical distractions such as notifications and social media and explain how they break focus.

concepts.name: Procrastination as avoidance
concepts.summary: Understand that procrastination is usually avoidance of discomfort rather than laziness.

misconceptions.text: Time management means filling every minute of the day with tasks.
Procrastination is simply laziness or a character flaw.
Keeping tasks in your head is enough if you are paying attention.

concepts.name: Prioritising with Eisenhower matrix
concepts.summary: Sort tasks into do, schedule, delegate and eliminate quadrants and act on each accordingly.

concepts.name: Time blocking
concepts.summary: Assign specific tasks to dedicated calendar blocks of time for the day.

concepts.name: Pomodoro technique
concepts.summary: Work in timed focus intervals separated by short breaks and longer breaks after several rounds.

concepts.name: Breaking tasks into steps
concepts.summary: Split vague large tasks into small concrete next actions that can be started immediately.

concepts.name: Daily planning routine
concepts.summary: Choose a few key priorities each day and plan them against the calendar.

concepts.name: Reducing distractions
concepts.summary: Apply tactics like muting notifications and clearing the workspace to protect focus.

concepts.name: Starting tactics against procrastination
concepts.summary: Use small starting commitments to overcome the resistance of beginning a task.

misconceptions.text: Everything urgent is important, so urgent tasks should always be done first.
A time-blocked schedule must be followed perfectly or it has failed.
Pomodoro breaks are wasted time that should be skipped when you feel productive.

concepts.name: Weekly planning and review
concepts.summary: Review the past week, clear inboxes and plan the next week's priorities against goals and calendar.

concepts.name: Context switching costs
concepts.summary: Analyse how switching between tasks reduces efficiency and arrange work to limit it.

concepts.name: Batching similar tasks
concepts.summary: Group similar low-focus tasks like email or errands into set sessions to cut context-switching costs.

concepts.name: Saying no and negotiating
concepts.summary: Decline, defer or renegotiate requests politely when they conflict with existing priorities.

concepts.name: Energy-aware scheduling
concepts.summary: Match demanding tasks to high-energy periods and routine tasks to low-energy ones.

concepts.name: Buffers and planning fallacy
concepts.summary: Explain why estimates run short and add buffers to absorb overruns and interruptions.

concepts.name: Diagnosing procrastination causes
concepts.summary: Identify whether a delayed task stems from unclear next steps, fear, boredom or low value, and choose a fix accordingly.

misconceptions.text: Multitasking lets you get more done than doing one thing at a time.
Saying no makes you unhelpful and damages relationships.
A weekly review is wasted time that could be spent on actual work.

concepts.name: Aligning time with goals
concepts.summary: Evaluate whether your calendar reflects long-term goals and reallocate time accordingly.

concepts.name: Auditing time use
concepts.summary: Track how time is actually spent and analyse gaps between plan and reality to find leaks.

concepts.name: Selecting system fit
concepts.summary: Judge which techniques suit a given role, workload and personality and adapt or drop those that do not.

concepts.name: Managing interruptions and availability
concepts.summary: Design norms for email, chat and meetings that balance responsiveness with deep work.

concepts.name: Delegation and elimination decisions
concepts.summary: Decide which tasks to delegate, automate or abandon based on value and cost.

concepts.name: Handling overload and replanning
concepts.summary: Triage and replan when workload exceeds capacity, renegotiating scope and deadlines.

concepts.name: Sustainable pace and recovery
concepts.summary: Analyse how rest, sleep and breaks affect output and plan them as part of the system.

misconceptions.text: Working longer hours always yields proportionally more output.
A productivity system that works for someone else will work for you unchanged.
Being instantly responsive to every message demonstrates good time management.

concepts.name: Designing a personal system
concepts.summary: Create an integrated system of capture, planning, review and focus practices tailored to your context.

concepts.name: Evaluating system effectiveness
concepts.summary: Assess a system by outcomes and wellbeing rather than activity and refine it using evidence.

concepts.name: Opportunity cost and strategic choice
concepts.summary: Evaluate commitments by what they displace and choose deliberately among competing good options.

concepts.name: Team and shared time design
concepts.summary: Create meeting, handoff and availability norms that protect focus time across a group.

concepts.name: Coaching others on time
concepts.summary: Diagnose another person's time problems and design tailored, realistic changes for them.

concepts.name: Adapting across life changes
concepts.summary: Judge when role, workload or life changes demand rebuilding routines rather than patching them.

misconceptions.text: The goal of time management is maximum efficiency and throughput at all times.
Once a system is built, it should be kept fixed for consistency.
Advice that helped you will work for anyone you coach.
